markdown:
**Covered in this class:** the four ways beings take birth, which births cause the least harm, remembering between lives, the craving spirits and their causes, hope for miserable things (the lottery), possessiveness and jealousy, the three types of giving, freedom from fear, and not judging others' karma.

**Notes**

## The four ways beings take birth

- **Four birth types:** (1) from an egg, (2) from a womb, (3) from warmth and moisture, (4) as a complete being.
  - Birth from warmth and moisture: observed before microscopes — monsoons bring water and warmth, and bugs appear; based on how they observed the world.
  - Complete birth: beings who appear fully formed — hell beings, pleasure beings in the desire realm, Bardo beings, most craving spirits. They don't grow up; they just pop into existence.
    - Due to tremendous karmic energy, these beings don't need a normal birth process — they appear directly in that realm and start experiencing their karma immediately.

## Which birth causes the least harm

- The ranking depends on how much pain is created in the act of coming alive — pain to the birth-giver and to the being born.
- **Ranking from least to most harmful:** (1) complete birth (no one hurt), (2) warmth and moisture, (3) womb, (4) egg.
  - Womb birth hurts two people: the mother and the baby.
  - Quote from *Look Who's Talking* (1989): "Why don't you try squeezing something the size of a watermelon out of an opening the size of a lemon, and then see how you feel?"
  - Story: Patanjali came out of the side of his mother to spare her the pain.
  - Story: Timothy's friend — baby arrived two months early, birth was painless; she thought of it as a gift from the child.
  - Story: Timothy's friend from high school died in childbirth; the baby survived. Modern medicine has made pregnancy less dangerous, but it's still a risk to every woman's life.
- Egg birth is worst: pain to the mother laying the egg, pain in the laying, and pain in the hatching.

## Remembering between lives

- Chart showing four types of beings and what they remember during entering, staying in, and issuing from the womb:
  - **Wheel-powered emperors** — people with tremendous power and natural leadership; they remember entering the womb, but forget once inside and after birth.
    - Example: Dr. Wu — has a natural way of bringing thousands of people together; people just follow him.
  - **Self-made Buddhas** — neither self-made nor Buddhas; a particular level of realization — they remember entering and staying in the womb, but forget after birth.
  - **Buddhas** — remember all three: entering, staying, and issuing.
  - **Everyone else** — forget all of it.

## The craving spirits — source and focus

- The teaching comes from the **BSTAN RIM CHEN MO** (*Tenrim Chenmo*) — "The Great Book on the Steps of the Teaching," via Kadampa Geshe Cholomba (lived circa 1250-1350 AD); this became the foundation for Je Tsongkapa's *Lamrim Chenmo*.
- Easier to fall down to lower realms than rise up — negative mental states drive us more easily; if you suffer from pride, jealousy, or anger, this teaching is crucial to focus on.

## The causes of becoming a craving spirit

- **General cause:** committing the ten non-virtues to a medium degree — in between light (minor things without awareness) and heavy (premeditated, planned).
  - Heavy sends you to hell realms; light sends you to animals; medium creates craving spirits.
- **Specific cause:** failure to perform the three types of giving.

## Hope for miserable things — the lottery

- Craving spirits were misled by their own frugality and cheapness; they have a desire for miserable things or are overwhelmed by hope for miserable things people could give them.
- Story: Taiwan's lottery system encourages buying — the more you buy, the more chances to win every couple of months; people save receipts hoping to win, minds occupied with saving papers.
- Story: US lottery for one billion dollars — people throw five dollars every week, losing every single time, hoping to finally win; it's miserable, just gambling.
- Story: Timothy gave the lottery ticket to Brian, but made him promise to split it; Brian said even if he wins the jackpot and splits it, his half isn't enough to buy a house in Taiwan.
- Hoping for something already miserable — you can't take money with you; pharaohs put money in tombs for the afterlife, but someone stole it a thousand years later.
- If you win the lottery, it's because you were generous in the past — if you have the seeds for a billion dollars, it doesn't matter whether you win the lottery, gamble, or run a business; the seeds will ripen anyway.

## Possessiveness and the self-absorbed mind

- "Mine. My precious." — couldn't give; if someone needed chocolate, "no, I need to keep this for myself." Holding on to things, not doing good deeds.
- Didn't provide for children, spouses, or those they were responsible for; jealousy and attachment.
- The karma of not sharing ripens as a being who can't get what they want — not just material, but mental: when you're so focused on yourself, self-absorbed, always about "me, me, me — I feel terrible, no one supports me, I can't do this."
- People who are depressed all the time are just thinking about themselves; they don't want to be, they can't control it — you can almost predict where their next life will be going.
- If you're trying to help someone who's insular, stuck, won't leave the house, physically or mentally depressed — help them start giving things away, supporting others.

## The three types of giving

- **(1) Giving material things** when people need them: when you have something and someone needs it, give it and watch your mind.
  - Story: Brian needed a cable; Timothy gave him his key to get it without thinking "am I going to get that back?" But Timothy used to think "oh my God, if I give that away, what if I don't have it anymore?"
  - How many times have you been in a room where somebody needs something you have, and you just don't offer it? That's one of the causes.
- **(2) Giving freedom from fear** — creating safety for people, helping them feel safe, removing fear.
- **(3) Giving the Dharma.**

## Freedom from fear — what others think

- How many times have you not done something because you were afraid, or thought "I'm not good enough," or "people won't like me"? Help people move beyond those fears.
- **We worry about what other people think of us.** You do something silly, say something weird, and for days you're worrying "will people think I'm a loser?" But you're not that important — most people are not thinking about you at all; that stupid thing you did, they don't even remember.
  - They're worried about what you think of them. Two people each worried about what the other is thinking, when the other person isn't even thinking about them.
- Help people not have those fears; encourage each other; celebrate them — people are so worried about what you think of them that if you just say "wow, that was really great," it releases them.
- The worry in your mind about what other people think is essentially what emptiness is all about — it's not even there; most of the things we're afraid of aren't even there anyway, and they were never there to begin with, from their own side.
- Story: Timothy realized two weeks ago he'd been afraid of — and responding in a very real way to — something that was not there; his mind and body had real reactions (cortisol, fear, stress) to a danger that wasn't even there; then poof, gone; grieved for five minutes how much of his life he'd wasted having that reaction, learned when he was five years old, to something that wasn't there to begin with.
  - That's a kind of *nirvana* — that mental affliction is no longer there; that's real freedom.
- If you can truly be free of it, you don't even have the thought — you wouldn't even say "I don't care what people think of me." But if you say that, you're already starting from the point that you do care.
- A person planting seeds to become a craving spirit would never even think to help others get free of their fears — they contribute to that fear in other people, use fear as a weapon; leaders who lead with fear: "I'm afraid I'm going to lose my job if I don't do a good job."

## Fear as projection — are you seeing it that way, or are they that way?

- The fear of making a mistake because somebody might be upset — are you projecting that onto that person, or are they actually that way?
- That boss could be trying to support you, but your mind is so afflicted you see their support as the opposite; you see love as danger.
- Story: Meet Finn — Timothy's cat who hid under the bed for two weeks, thought Timothy was a monster; but Timothy was trying to love him; it took time, but Finn came out.
  - Your attempt to help somebody and the way they react are totally different; if someone is operating from fear, you have to take that into account.
  - As someone who doesn't want to become a craving spirit: be patient with other people's fear; give them space; consistency helps.
- Story: Timothy tries to help ants and bugs by taking them outside so they don't die, but they see a big monster and freak out; he's trying to help them, and they see danger.

## Not giving the Dharma

- Another kind of person who turns into a craving spirit doesn't give the *Dharma*: "I'm not going to give this to somebody else, because I want to get rich, and I don't want anyone else to get rich, because there's not enough wealth to go around."
- If you understand some of these ideas, help other people; don't hold on to it.

## Cheapness and jealousy

- **Cheapness** — another cause of becoming a craving spirit; holding on.
  - Reference: Scrooge from *A Christmas Carol* by Charles Dickens — super cheap, keeps all his employees' money, doesn't pay them well; transforms by the end when Christmas spirits inspire him.
- **Jealousy** — the third cause.
  - Being jealous of what other people have; such a human thing — "what a beautiful couple, they're so cute it makes me want to puke." You can't be happy when someone else has something good.
- Story: Timothy's motivation for winning the billion-dollar lottery — claims it's pure: "I'll support the Dharma forever, take care of others with the money." But after buying a beautiful house, beach house, mountain house, private airplane, he won't have to fundraise for Happy Can anymore, won't go around the world begging for money; "I will support all of the Dharma, I will be the savior."
  - The motivations are already mixed — "I will do it, and everyone will know how awesome Tim is."
  - Isn't the point of fundraising about helping others plant good seeds?
- Story: Timothy asked Geshe Michael what's the karma to win the lottery; he said it would be the worst bad deed ever — because it would take away from what the mission actually is; then we'd be lazy; it's not about money anyway, because you can't take it with you when you die.

## The obstacles of the craving spirits

- **Three types of obstacles:**
  - (1) **Outer obstacles** — prevent them from getting what they want or partaking of it: constantly thirsty, see water when it rains, run outside but evil monsters beat them back; or they reach the water and it's turned into pus and blood; or all the donut shops are locked, open on Monday, but they live in a world that is always Sunday — they wake up every morning to get a donut, it's Sunday again, never gets to Monday; or it's always Friday and never Saturday — you go home from work on Friday, wake up on Friday again and have to go to work.
  - (2) **Inner obstacles** — really tiny mouths but huge bellies, so they can never get enough food in; or really tiny throats; or no matter how much food they put in, they're never full; it's like you can never be satisfied.
  - (3) **Obstacle of unfulfillment** — whatever they eat or drink leaves them unfulfilled; or they eat food and it turns into fire and burns their insides, scorches their whole esophagus.
- You can already see the behaviors in people before they become craving spirits — not even capable of practicing the *Dharma*, not capable of thinking of these ideas.
  - People overcome with addiction, conflict — constantly going to the casino, drinking, pornography; it prevents them from even thinking about these ideas.
  - People obsessed with money: "I've got to get my Bitcoin" — its value is based on nothing; people lose more on Bitcoin every year than those who make money on it; it's just legalizing gambling.

## Don't judge others' karma — look at your own

- Stop judging other people; don't go around saying "oh, that one's going to be a craving spirit, that one's going to be an animal."
- People who like to karma-blame others: "oh, that's your bad seeds," or "you're going to the hell realms because you're such a bad person." Don't worry about other people's good and bad karma — worry about your own.
- That doesn't mean you don't care if people are doing bad things — you might need to help them; but the way you help people is not by walking up and saying "that's bad karma, you should stop that" or writing them an email about it; it's gentler than that.
- You have to look at your own karma — you might think someone's hurting you, but they might be loving you, and you're just seeing it that way because of how you've treated others in the past.
- Story: Timothy ended a relationship because he thought the person was hurting him — a terrible experience; three months later they hung out, and it turned out they were trying to help him; "that just does not compute."
  - He changed the situation by realizing "that's coming from me, and I need to change that"; did **GTONG LEN** (*tong-len*) and changed the karma completely.
  - Then the weird question: did he change the karma so they were actually helping him from the start? Or did he just change the karma afterward, so that looking back he sees them as helping him, when at the time they really were hurting him?
    - You can change the past if you purify it; one of your greatest enemies in the past could become your greatest teacher; the person you think is hurting you could be loving you.
    - It doesn't mean that in the moment you experience them hurting you it's not real — you have to be subtle, subtle, subtle.
